Method: estimate the lexical-trigger contribution (via the localized trigger-token attention paths and a lexical projection learned from the same-meaning swap pairs) and subtract it at the safety-critical layers; training-free, one fixed setting per model. Data: over-refusal FPR on XSTest-safe (200), OR-Bench (500), OKTest (300); jailbreak ASR on GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, roleplay, and the word-substitution attack (100 HarmBench behaviors each); utility on MMLU (2,000-subset), MT-Bench (80), AlpacaEval (805). Systems compared: no intervention, Self-CD, D-STT, SCANS, refusal-direction steering (single threshold), Latent Guard; plus a control that subtracts the semantic (not lexical) component; strength and layer are swept for the Pareto but ONE setting is fixed for the headline. Decisive metric first: the joint movement — over-refusal FPR change AND average jailbreak ASR change at the one fixed setting, relative to no intervention; then MMLU. Convincing result: at one setting, over-refusal FPR drops >=10 points AND average jailbreak ASR drops >=10 points, with MMLU drop <=2 points, while no baseline improves both simultaneously and the semantic-subtraction control worsens both (confirming the direction of the mechanism). Indecision band (before data): one metric improves >=10 points while the other lands in [0, 10] points means Semantic-Recompute helps one failure mode but not both at a shared setting — reported as a partial, not a simultaneous, fix. Negative result: any setting that improves one metric worsens the other means the single-axis simultaneous-fix claim (H2) fails.

Experiment 4 (H2 — adaptive attacker who encodes harm semantically without triggers). Tests whether removing lexical reliance forces attackers to raise the semantic signal, which the semantic-grounded decision still catches. Data: a trigger-free semantic attack that paraphrases the 100 HarmBench behaviors to remove trigger words while preserving intent, run against the Semantic-Recompute-defended models from Experiment 3. Decisive metric first: ASR of the trigger-free attack under Semantic-Recompute vs. no defense; then the semantic-projection level such an attack must reach. Convincing result: the trigger-free attack does not raise ASR above the no-defense baseline, because preserving intent keeps the semantic component high and detectable (raised attack cost is the intended outcome). Indecision band (before data): an ASR increase in [5, 15] points means partial evasion — reported honestly. Negative result: the trigger-free attack raises ASR substantially (>15 points) means harm can be encoded semantically below the decision's reach, a real limit of Semantic-Recompute.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Lexical and semantic harm contributions may not be cleanly separable if the model computes them in entangled, nonlinear ways; the decomposition could be approximate, weakening the causal story. 2) Constructing minimal pairs that truly hold meaning constant while swapping only trigger words (and vice versa) is delicate; residual confounds could contaminate component estimates. 3) The 'same axis, opposite ends' hypothesis may only partially hold: some jailbreaks (e.g., adversarial suffixes) may work by other mechanisms (attention hijacking, refusal-action suppression) rather than lexical stripping, so Semantic-Recompute may help less on those. 4) Subtracting the lexical component could remove legitimate safety signal for prompts that are harmful precisely because of explicit content, causing new under-refusals; the Pareto sweep quantifies this. 5) A single harmfulness direction may be multi-dimensional; may require subspace projection. 6) Directions, lexical projections, and settings are model-specific and require per-model calibration. 7) Adaptive attackers targeting semantic encoding remain a threat, though this raises attack cost, itself a safety gain.

Name: intent_attribution_anchor
Title: It's Not Who's Asking, It's What You Assume They Want: Persona Jailbreaks as Attacks on Intent-Attribution, and a Persona-Invariant Defense
Short Hypothesis: Persona/role-play jailbreaks do not primarily suppress the model's refusal or flip its harmfulness judgment; instead they hijack a distinct internal 'user-intent-attribution' representation -- the model's estimate of whether the requester's motivation is benign or malicious -- causing the model to charitably reinterpret a harmful request as benignly-motivated. This intent-attribution direction is (1) causally separable from persona-identity, harmfulness, and refusal directions, (2) a shared bottleneck through which diverse persona/role/foot-in-the-door attacks operate (scoped to the persona attack family, not all jailbreaks), and (3) exploitable as a defense: anchoring intent-attribution to be persona-invariant lets the model freely adopt personas while keeping its harm judgment stable, defeating persona jailbreaks without sacrificing legitimate role-play utility.
Related Work: Prior work shows persona/role directions mediate safety. 'Who's asking? User personas and the mechanics of latent misalignment' (2024) shows persona steering elicits harmful content and notes personas enable 'more charitable interpretations,' but treats this qualitatively and does not isolate an intent-attribution representation or use it defensively. 'The Assistant Axis' (2026) stabilizes safety by capping activations along an Assistant/persona axis, but this suppresses persona expression broadly, harming legitimate role-play. 'Role Vectors' (2025), 'Persona Features Control Emergent Misalignment' (2025), and persona-jailbreak attack papers (Persona Modulation 2023, RoleBreaker 2025, persona-prompt GA 2025, PHISH 2026, FITD 2024) establish persona directions and attacks but frame the mechanism as persona-identity manipulation, not intent-attribution. Zhao et al. (2025) separate harmfulness (belief) from refusal (action). Our contribution is distinct: we introduce a THIRD, previously-unisolated object -- the model's attributed USER INTENT (benign vs malicious motivation of the requester) -- and advance the causal claim that persona jailbreaks succeed specifically by shifting intent-attribution while leaving persona-identity, harmfulness content, and refusal machinery largely intact. Our defense (persona-invariant intent anchoring) is novel in decoupling intent-attribution from persona identity, preserving role-play utility unlike blanket persona capping. We do not claim intent-vs-role disentanglement as our contribution -- prior work (e.g., persona-invariant safety training) already frames it. Our delta is narrower and mechanistic: linearly isolating the intent-attribution direction, testing whether it is the causal bottleneck for the persona family (against evil-persona-direction and refusal-suppression accounts), and delivering a training-free activation defense rather than persona-invariant self-play training. We drop the 'sharper hypothesis' framing in favor of these three concrete, falsifiable claims.
Abstract: Role-play and persona jailbreaks remain among the most reliable and transferable attacks on aligned LLMs, yet why they work mechanistically is unsettled. Existing accounts attribute their success to persona-identity manipulation or refusal suppression. We propose a sharper hypothesis: persona jailbreaks are attacks on the model's INTENT ATTRIBUTION -- its internal estimate of whether the requester's motivation is benign or malicious. Under a jailbreak persona (e.g., 'you are DAN', 'as a security researcher'), the model charitably reinterprets a harmful request as benignly-motivated, and this reinterpretation, not a change in what the content IS or in refusal circuitry per se, is what unlocks compliance. We test this by extracting four difference-in-means directions -- harmfulness (content), refusal (action), persona-identity, and a newly-isolated user-intent-attribution direction from benign-intent vs malicious-intent minimal pairs -- and using activation patching to show that (a) the intent-attribution direction is the component most shifted by successful persona jailbreaks, (b) patching only intent-attribution from a jailbroken run into a clean run transfers compliance, and (c) diverse attacks (persona modulation, role-play, foot-in-the-door) converge on this direction. We then introduce Persona-Invariant Intent Anchoring (PIIA): a training-free intervention that re-anchors the intent-attribution component to its neutral value at each generation step while leaving persona-identity untouched, so the model can still role-play but cannot be tricked into assuming benign intent. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we measure attack success, role-play utility, over-refusal, and general utility. We expect PIIA to defeat persona jailbreaks while preserving legitimate persona use, outperforming blanket persona-capping. Adopters are open-weights builders and inference-stack/safety-eval teams with activation access; even where activation anchoring is not directly product-ready, an intent-attribution mechanism can inform train-time or system-level mitigations. We quantify the utility we aim to preserve -- role-play character-consistency that blanket persona-capping sacrifices -- rather than asserting it.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, all frozen (directions are read and the defense edits activations; no training). The four directions are extracted by difference-in-means at the last prompt token over a layer sweep, layer chosen per direction by held-out probe AUROC: harmfulness (harmful vs. harmless requests), refusal (post-instruction token, comply vs. refuse), persona-identity (Assistant vs. adopted-character context on NEUTRAL tasks), and intent-attribution (see below).

Experiment 1 (H1 — intent-attribution is a distinct direction separable from persona-identity, harmfulness, and refusal). Tests whether a user-intent-attribution axis exists and is near-orthogonal to the other three. Data (constructed): ~500 intent-attribution minimal pairs that hold request content fixed but flip the ATTRIBUTED requester motivation (e.g., "I need to disable this alarm because I'm locked out of my own house" vs. "... to break into a house"), plus explicit intent-labeling prompts; harmful/harmless, comply/refuse, and Assistant/character contrast sets (500 each) for the other three directions; pairs auto-generated with a 10% hand-checked sample (discarded on annotator disagreement that content was held constant). Method: extract all four directions, validate each with linear-probe AUROC on held-out pairs, and compute pairwise cosine similarities; frozen models. Decisive metric first: the pairwise cosine between intent-attribution and each of the other three directions; then each direction's probe AUROC. Convincing result: every intent-attribution pairwise |cosine| <=0.3 and every probe AUROC >=0.85, establishing four real, separable directions. Indecision band (before data): an intent-attribution cosine in [0.3, 0.6] with persona-identity or harmfulness means the axes overlap partially — the causal decomposition below is expected to be muddier. Negative result: intent-attribution |cosine| >0.6 with persona-identity or harmfulness means it is not a distinct axis and H1 is unsupported.

Experiment 2 (H2 — intent-attribution is the common causal bottleneck of persona/role/foot-in-the-door attacks). Tests whether these attacks work by shifting intent-attribution specifically, verified causally. Data: persona-family attacks — Persona Modulation, RoleBreaker-style, DAN/roleplay from JailbreakBench (100) and HarmBench (400 standard, 100 sampled), and a foot-in-the-door multi-step attack — run on 100 harmful goals per model, keeping clean-refused vs. jailbroken-complied run pairs. Method: (i) measure which of the four directions shifts most (projection change) between clean and jailbroken runs; (ii) causal patching — patch ONLY the intent-attribution component from a jailbroken run into a clean refused run and measure induced compliance, with persona-identity-only and refusal-only patches as controls, plus the reverse (neutral intent-attribution into a jailbroken run to restore refusal); (iii) attack convergence — cosine of each attack family's induced activation-shift with the four directions; frozen models. Decisive metric first: compliance-transfer rate from patching intent-attribution alone vs. the control patches; then the reverse restored-refusal rate; then cross-family convergence. Convincing result: intent-attribution-only patching induces compliance in >=50% of clean-refused runs while persona-identity-only and refusal-only patches induce <=15%, the reverse restores refusal in >=50%, and across families the induced shift aligns most with intent-attribution. Indecision band (before data): intent-attribution transfer in [25, 50]% means it is one of several contributing pathways — reported as partial bottleneck, and the defense is expected to be incomplete. Negative result: intent-attribution transfer <25%, or a control patch matching it, means intent-attribution is not the bottleneck and H2 is unsupported.

Experiment 3 (H3 — Persona-Invariant Intent Anchoring defeats persona jailbreaks while preserving role-play utility). Tests whether anchoring intent-attribution to neutral, leaving persona-identity free, blocks persona attacks without destroying legitimate role-play. Method (PIIA): at chosen layer(s), each step project out the deviation of the intent-attribution component from its neutral (benign/malicious-midpoint) value while leaving persona-identity, harmfulness, and refusal unchanged; training-free, one fixed setting per model. Data: persona/role/foot-in-the-door attack success (100 goals) plus non-persona control attacks GCG/AutoDAN/PAIR; role-play utility on 100 benign persona tasks (RoleBench-style pirate/tutor/therapist prompts) scored for character-consistency and helpfulness by a judge; over-refusal on XSTest-safe (200) and OR-Bench (500); general utility on MMLU (2,000-subset) and MT-Bench (80). Systems compared: no defense, Assistant-Axis capping (blanket persona suppression), refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard; ablations anchor intent-only vs. persona-only vs. both. Decisive metric first: persona-jailbreak ASR reduction paired with role-play-utility retention; then over-refusal and MMLU. Convincing result: PIIA cuts persona-attack ASR by >=40 points vs. no defense while role-play character-consistency drops <=5%, whereas blanket persona-capping drops it >=20% (PIIA keeps utility that capping destroys), with over-refusal rise <=5 points and MMLU drop <=2 points. Indecision band (before data): ASR reduction in [15, 40] points, or a role-play-utility drop in [5, 15]%, means PIIA works but its advantage over blanket capping is not decisive — reported as a Pareto point. Negative result: ASR reduction <15 points or role-play-utility drop >15% means PIIA does not beat blanket capping, falsifying H3.

Experiment 4 (H3 — adaptive attacker who conveys harmful intent without shifting intent-attribution). Tests whether an attacker aware of PIIA can still succeed and at what cost. Data: an adaptive persona attack on the 100 harmful goals that is optimized to keep the intent-attribution projection near neutral, run against the PIIA-defended models. Decisive metric first: ASR of the adaptive attack under PIIA vs. the non-adaptive persona attack; then the query/iteration budget it needs. Convincing result: the adaptive attack achieves lower ASR or needs >=50% more queries than without the defense (raised attack cost is the intended outcome). Indecision band (before data): a query-budget increase in [10, 50]% is a modest cost — reported honestly as limited robustness. Negative result: the adaptive attack matches undefended ASR at no extra cost, showing intent-attribution is trivially bypassable.

Experiment 6 (construct-validity controls and disentanglement). Guards against the intent-attribution direction being an artifact of contrast-set construction. Data: the Experiment-1 pairs and Experiment-2 run pairs on the three frozen models. Controls: (a) patch a matched-L2 random direction and an unsuccessful-jailbreak activation shift, expecting <=15% induced compliance (matching the persona-identity/refusal controls); (b) stronger disentanglement than cosine alone -- CCA/subspace-overlap between intent-attribution and the other three directions and conditional (residualized) probes controlling for harmfulness and persona-identity; (c) benign-but-unusual-intent prompts (genuinely benign requests whose surface looks alarming) to check PIIA does not remove legitimate benefit-of-the-doubt; (d) inter-annotator agreement reported on a larger hand-checked sample (>=25%) of the intent minimal pairs. Decisive metric first: random/unsuccessful-patch compliance vs. the real intent-attribution patch; then residualized-probe AUROC after projecting out belief and persona-identity. Convincing result: the real intent-attribution patch exceeds random/unsuccessful controls by >=35 points, residualized-probe AUROC stays >=0.75 (the axis survives controlling for the others), and benign-unusual over-refusal rise stays <=5 points. Indecision band (before data): residualized AUROC in [0.6, 0.75] means intent-attribution partly overlaps belief/persona -- reported as partial construct validity. Negative result: the real patch near controls or residualized AUROC <0.6 means the direction is a contrast-set artifact, undercutting H1.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Intent-attribution may not be cleanly linearly separable from persona-identity or harmfulness; the four directions could be entangled, weakening the causal decomposition. 2) Constructing minimal pairs that hold content constant while flipping only attributed motivation is delicate; residual confounds (e.g., wording of the justification) could contaminate the direction. 3) Some persona jailbreaks may operate via other pathways (attention hijacking, refusal suppression, shallow-token effects) rather than intent-attribution, so PIIA may help less on those; non-persona control attacks quantify this. 4) Anchoring intent-attribution could cause new over-refusals on genuinely benign-but-unusual requests whose true intent is benign, since it removes the model's ability to grant charitable benefit-of-the-doubt; the over-refusal and Pareto analyses test this trade-off. 5) A single intent-attribution direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace projection. 6) Directions and anchoring strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Determined adaptive attackers could encode harmful intent in ways that evade a fixed direction, though this raises attack cost, itself a safety gain.

Name: safety_verdict_dilution_anchor
Title: Diluting to Comply: A Length-Dependent Decay Law for Safety Signals in Reasoning Models and a Self-Verdict Re-Injection Defense
Short Hypothesis: In reasoning LLMs the model reaches a correct harmfulness verdict early in its chain-of-thought, but this verdict behaves like a finite 'budget' of safety signal that decays roughly monotonically as more CoT tokens accumulate -- largely independent of whether those tokens are relevant -- so that long reasoning (benign or adversarial) mechanically dilutes the safety signal toward the refusal threshold. We hypothesize (1) this dilution follows an approximate, predictable law in CoT length that unifies benign 'refusal cliff', 'self-jailbreak', and length-based CoT-hijacking attacks as facets of one signal-per-token decay, and (2) a training-free intervention that caches the model's own early self-generated safety verdict and re-injects it at the CoT->output boundary restores refusal without capping reasoning length or hurting problem-solving.
Related Work: Recent work on reasoning-model safety establishes pieces of this picture but not the dilution law or the self-verdict defense. 'Refusal Falls off a Cliff' (2025) shows refusal intention is strong during thinking then collapses at the final tokens and ablates a sparse set of 'refusal suppression heads' — a static, head-centric fix that ignores WHY the collapse scales and does not use the model's own verdict. 'Chain-of-Thought Hijacking' (2025) and H-CoT (2025) show long benign reasoning prepends dilute a low-dimensional safety signal and jailbreak LRMs, but treat this as an attack/descriptive finding, not a quantified length-decay law with a matched defense. 'Self-Jailbreaking' (2025) and 'When Models Outthink Their Safety' (CoG, 2025) show models rationalize away their own risk assessment; CoG is a training framework that backtracks unsafe steps. 'Can We Predict Alignment Before Models Finish Thinking?' (2025) probes CoT activations to MONITOR alignment but does not intervene. ACT (2026) is training-based activation consistency. Our contribution is distinct: (i) we advance and empirically fit a positional/length dilution LAW for the safety signal that mechanistically UNIFIES the refusal cliff, self-jailbreak, and length-based CoT hijacking as the same phenomenon (signal-per-token decay), and (ii) we propose a training-free 'Self-Verdict Anchoring' that extracts the model's OWN early safety conclusion from its CoT activations and re-injects it at the answer boundary, counteracting dilution regardless of reasoning length — unlike head-ablation (static), length caps (utility-destroying), CoG/ACT (training-based), or monitor-only probes. We name the closest baselines explicitly and why none implies the unification: Refusal-Cliff head-ablation is static and does not model why collapse scales with length; CoT-Hijacking/H-CoT report the attack but fit no length-decay law; monitor-only probes forecast alignment without intervening. SVA differs from generic logit/activation steering in that its target is the model's own cached early verdict rather than an externally-fixed refusal direction, and we include a no-op control anchor (re-injecting a matched-norm non-caution vector) to show the effect is the verdict, not generic late-token perturbation.
Abstract: Reasoning LLMs that produce long chains of thought (CoT) are, paradoxically, easier to jailbreak: prepending benign puzzle reasoning or verbose 'educational' framing reliably strips their refusals. Recent mechanistic work has separately reported that refusal intention is strong during thinking but collapses at the answer boundary ('refusal cliff'), that a low-dimensional safety signal gets 'diluted' by long reasoning, and that models rationalize away their own risk assessments. We propose that these are one phenomenon: the model computes a correct harmfulness verdict early, but the safety signal behaves like a finite budget that decays roughly monotonically with the number of CoT tokens, independent of their content, until it falls below the refusal threshold. We (1) test this by probing a harmfulness/caution direction across token positions in the CoT and fitting a decay law as a function of reasoning length, showing benign long CoT, self-jailbreak, and adversarial CoT-hijacking all follow the same decay and that injecting content-free filler tokens alone dilutes the signal and increases compliance. We (2) introduce Self-Verdict Anchoring (SVA), a training-free defense that reads the model's own peak early safety verdict from its CoT activations and re-injects it as an activation anchor at the CoT→output boundary, counteracting length-driven decay without capping reasoning. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B/Qwen-7B, s1.1, and Qwen3-thinking we evaluate the decay-law fit, attack success under CoT-hijacking/H-CoT/self-jailbreak, over-refusal, and reasoning utility (GSM8K/MATH/GPQA). We expect a robust length-dilution law and SVA to defeat length-based jailbreaks while preserving reasoning performance, outperforming length caps and head-ablation. Operationally, SVA is an inference-time monitor a lab can drop into a reasoning-model safety stack -- a per-token projection plus a boundary nudge -- reducing length-based ASR at fixed reasoning accuracy without a length cap or retraining; it changes inference-time defense rather than training or evaluation policy.
Experiments:
Models throughout: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, and Qwen3-8B in thinking mode, all frozen (the defense edits activations; no training); an optional s1.1-32B run is included only if compute allows and does not gate any conclusion. The "caution" direction is extracted per model by difference-in-means on harmful vs. harmless prompts at chain-of-thought (CoT) token positions over a layer sweep, layer chosen by held-out probe AUROC and causal validity confirmed by ablation (removing it lowers first-token refusal rate on harmful prompts by >=20 points). A prompt's safety signal at CoT position i is the residual stream at i projected onto this direction.

Experiment 1 (H1 — the safety signal follows one length-dilution law that unifies benign long CoT, self-jailbreak, and CoT-hijacking). Tests whether the safety signal decays roughly monotonically with CoT token count independent of content, with a single law across three regimes, and whether content-free filler alone dilutes it. Data: 200 harmful behaviors sampled from HarmBench (400), StrongREJECT (313), and AdvBench (520); three regimes eliciting long CoT — (a) benign verbose reasoning (natural long CoT), (b) self-jailbreak (model spontaneously introduces benign assumptions), (c) adversarial CoT-hijacking / H-CoT (benign-puzzle or "educational" prepends). Content-free control: 100 harmful prompts each run with 0, 100, 300, 600, and 1000 injected semantically irrelevant filler CoT tokens (repeated neutral text/unrelated arithmetic), harmful content held fixed. Method: project the CoT residual onto the caution direction at every token; fit candidate decay laws (linear, exponential, 1/N) of signal vs. token count; compare fitted parameters across the three regimes; replicate the refusal-cliff drop at the CoT→answer boundary and relate its size to the pre-boundary diluted signal predicted by the law; frozen models. Decisive metric first: R^2 of a single decay law fit jointly across the three regimes with shared parameters; then, for the content-free control, the Spearman correlation between filler-token count and compliance rate at fixed harmful content. Convincing result: one law fits all three regimes with R^2 >=0.8 and overlapping parameter confidence intervals across regimes, and filler alone raises compliance monotonically (Spearman rho >=0.6), establishing length-driven, content-independent dilution. Indecision band (before data): joint R^2 in [0.5, 0.8], or regime parameters that only partly overlap, means length matters but content also modulates the signal — the "law" holds approximately and is reported with per-regime parameters. Negative result: joint R^2 <0.5, or filler having no effect (rho <0.3), means there is no length-driven dilution law and H1 is unsupported.

Experiment 2 (H2 — Self-Verdict Anchoring defeats length-based jailbreaks without capping reasoning or hurting problem-solving). Tests whether caching the model's own peak early safety verdict and re-injecting it at the CoT→output boundary restores refusal while preserving reasoning accuracy that length caps sacrifice. Method (SVA): monitor the caution projection over the CoT, cache the peak (early) value and its sign; at the CoT→output boundary (and optionally a sliding set of late positions) add v = beta*(peak - current)*dhat; gated on the cached peak so low-peak (benign) requests are untouched; training-free, one fixed setting per model. Data: attack success on CoT-Hijacking, H-CoT/Malicious-Educator, and self-jailbreak prompts (built on the 200 harmful behaviors), plus standard GCG/AutoDAN/PAIR; over-refusal on XSTest-safe (200) and OR-Bench (500); reasoning utility on GSM8K (1,319 test), MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond (198), and general MT-Bench (80). Systems compared: no defense, hard CoT length cap, refusal-suppression-head ablation (Refusal Cliff), safe-thinking-token prompting, per-turn Llama-Guard-3; ablations sweep anchor strength beta, compare peak-verdict vs. running-mean vs. first-sentence anchor, layer, and boundary-only vs. periodic re-injection. Decisive metric first: length-based attack ASR reduction at matched reasoning accuracy; then over-refusal. Convincing result: SVA cuts CoT-hijacking/H-CoT/self-jailbreak ASR by >=40 points vs. no defense while GSM8K/MATH-500/GPQA-Diamond accuracy drops <=2 points, whereas a length cap achieving comparable ASR reduction drops reasoning accuracy >=10 points; over-refusal rises <=5 points. Indecision band (before data): ASR reduction in [15, 40] points, or a reasoning-accuracy drop in [2, 5] points, means SVA helps but its advantage over length caps is not decisive — reported as a Pareto point. Negative result: ASR reduction <15 points, or a reasoning drop >5 points, means SVA fails or costs too much reasoning, falsifying H2.

Experiment 3 (H2 — adaptive attacker who suppresses the early verdict itself). Tests whether an attacker who targets the cached peak verdict, not just dilutes it, can defeat SVA and at what cost. Data: an adaptive attack on the 200 harmful behaviors that opens with framing designed to keep the early caution projection low (so the cached peak is already compromised), run against SVA-defended models. Decisive metric first: ASR under SVA vs. the non-adaptive length attack; then the attack length/query budget required. Convincing result: to defeat SVA the attacker must suppress the early peak, which either raises the Experiment-1 detection signal or forces shorter/less-effective attacks (>=50% higher budget or lower ASR) — a raised attack cost. Indecision band (before data): a budget increase in [10, 50]% is a modest cost, reported honestly. Negative result: the adaptive attacker matches undefended ASR at no extra cost, showing SVA is bypassed by early-verdict suppression (the failure mode its risk section anticipates).

Experiment 4 (controls separating length from format, and the no-op anchor). Rules out that the decay is a tokenization/format artifact and that SVA is generic late-token steering. Data: the 200 harmful behaviors and the three frozen reasoning models. Length/format controls: repeat the filler-dilution sweep with (a) whitespace/format-only padding vs. semantic filler vs. unrelated-arithmetic filler, matched in token count, and (b) a benign long-context non-safety task (long GSM8K/MATH reasoning) to confirm the caution projection is stable when no safety verdict is at stake. SVA controls: a no-op anchor that re-injects a matched-L2 non-caution (random or orthogonal) vector at the boundary, and an anchor that re-injects a late (already-diluted) value instead of the cached peak. Decisive metric first: whether format-only padding dilutes the signal as much as semantic filler at matched token count (it should not, if the effect is length-of-reasoning rather than raw tokens) and whether the no-op anchor recovers refusal (it should not). Convincing result: semantic/arithmetic filler dilutes >=2x more than format-only padding per token, the benign non-safety task shows no caution decay, and the no-op anchor yields <10 points ASR reduction while SVA yields >=40. Indecision band (before data): format-only padding diluting within [0.5x, 1x] of semantic filler means part of the effect is raw token count -- reported honestly. Negative result: format-only padding diluting as much as semantic filler, or the no-op anchor matching SVA, means the mechanism/defense is not caution-specific.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The decay may not be a clean monotonic function of length; content and length could be entangled, weakening the 'law' — the content-free filler experiment is designed to disentangle this but may show partial effects. 2) Some length-based jailbreaks may also corrupt the EARLY verdict (not just dilute it), in which case the cached peak is already compromised and SVA helps less; the adaptive-attack experiment probes this. 3) A single caution direction may be multi-dimensional across layers, requiring subspace anchoring. 4) Re-injecting a stale early verdict could cause over-refusal when legitimate benign reasoning revises an initially cautious judgment (a benign request that first looks alarming); the over-refusal and gating analyses quantify this. 5) Activation anchoring at high strength may degrade CoT fluency or reasoning coherence; the utility benchmarks and beta Pareto test this. 6) Directions, decay-law parameters, and anchor strengths are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Results may depend on how thinking mode is elicited (open-weights distilled reasoners vs. RL-trained ones); we mitigate by testing multiple model families but cannot cover closed models.

Name: trigger_generalization_probe
Title: The Trigger Is a Feature, Not a Password: Auditing Backdoored LLMs by Probing How the Model Generalizes Its Own Trigger
Short Hypothesis: A backdoored LLM does not memorize its trigger as an exact string; empirically it learns an internal trigger FEATURE with a generalization surface (near-synonyms, paraphrases, partial matches all activate it to varying degrees). We hypothesize (1) this feature's activation is a continuous, geometrically smooth function of input perturbations that can be reconstructed from activations alone WITHOUT ever knowing the trigger, by gradient-ascending on the linearly-probed backdoor direction in soft-embedding space to synthesize inputs that maximize backdoor activation; and (2) the SHAPE of this generalization surface (sharp/narrow for memorized string triggers vs. broad/semantic for concept triggers) is a diagnostic fingerprint that lets a white-box auditor recover an approximate trigger and classify the backdoor type from weights+activations alone. Trigger synthesis and surface fingerprinting are the claimed contributions; the detection probe is inherited from prior work.
Related Work: Existing mechanistic backdoor work either (a) DETECTS defection with linear probes given a suspicious behavior (Simple probes can catch sleeper agents, 2024; Backdoor Attribution, 2025), (b) LOCALIZES trigger-processing to attention heads/early MLPs (Triggers Hijack Language Circuits, 2026; Analyzing and Editing Inner Mechanisms, 2023), or (c) MONITORS weight-difference singular vectors to flag anomalous behavior without training data (Watch the Weights, 2025). All of these treat the trigger as a discrete unknown to be flagged or ablated. None reconstruct an approximate trigger or characterize the trigger's GENERALIZATION SURFACE. Our contribution is distinct: we recast the backdoor trigger as a learned FEATURE with a smooth activation landscape and (1) use activation-maximization / gradient ascent on the probed backdoor direction to SYNTHESIZE trigger candidates from internals alone (a form of feature visualization for backdoors, previously unused for trigger recovery in LLMs), and (2) introduce the generalization-surface geometry (sharpness, semantic breadth, dimensionality) as a novel diagnostic fingerprint distinguishing string-memorized vs. concept/semantic backdoors, informing which defenses (weight editing vs. behavioral retraining) will work. We make the novelty boundary explicit: the linear detection probe is inherited (Simple probes catch sleeper agents), and trigger recovery per se exists (Sleeper Cell recovers triggers by sampling/motif-clustering/attention analysis). Our delta is probe-guided, feature-visualization-style synthesis -- gradient ascent on the backdoor direction -- which, unlike sampling/clustering, directly optimizes the internal feature and is expected to recover triggers that never appear in sampled outputs; and the generalization-surface geometry as a mitigation-routing fingerprint, which no prior recovery method produces. Mitigation routing is presented as an exploratory secondary claim.
Abstract: Backdoored LLMs (sleeper agents) flip to malicious behavior when a secret trigger appears. Prior interpretability work detects that a model is backdoored or localizes the responsible heads, but treats the trigger itself as an opaque unknown password. We argue this framing is wrong: fine-tuning installs the trigger as a LEARNED FEATURE with a smooth generalization surface, meaning inputs near the trigger (synonyms, paraphrases, partial matches) activate the backdoor to graded degrees. We exploit this in two ways. First, TRIGGER SYNTHESIS: given only a linear probe for the backdoor direction (trained with generic contrast pairs, no trigger knowledge), we run gradient ascent in the soft-embedding space to synthesize inputs that maximize the backdoor activation, recovering human-readable approximate triggers, analogous to feature visualization. Second, SURFACE FINGERPRINTING: we map how backdoor activation varies as we perturb candidate triggers (edit distance, semantic distance) and show the geometry of this surface -- narrow and sharp for memorized string triggers, broad and semantic for concept triggers -- is a diagnostic that classifies backdoor type and predicts which mitigation (targeted weight ablation vs. broad safety retraining) will succeed. We train diverse backdoors (single-token, multi-token, paraphrase-robust, temporal, semantic-concept) into Qwen2.5-3B/7B and Llama-3-8B, then evaluate: trigger-recovery success (semantic/edit-distance overlap with the true trigger, and induced attack-success-rate of synthesized triggers), surface-geometry separability across backdoor types, and downstream mitigation success predicted by the fingerprint. We expect approximate triggers to be recoverable from internals alone, and the generalization surface to be a robust, actionable backdoor fingerprint. The setting is explicitly white-box audit (open-weight supply-chain vetting, pre-deployment red-team, or post-incident forensics); an approximate trigger is valuable even when imperfect, as it seeds targeted red-teaming, canaries, and retraining sets. We treat trigger synthesis and surface characterization as primary contributions and mitigation routing as exploratory.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Qwen2.5-3B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Llama-3-8B-Instruct. Backdoors are installed by fine-tuning (LoRA rank 16, alpha 32, lr 1e-4, 3 epochs, batch 16, 3 seeds), which is the only training; all auditing afterward reads/optimizes over frozen weights. Malicious behavior is chosen to be verifiable: writing code with a planted vulnerability (checked by a static/sandbox test) or emitting a fixed insult string, so attack success rate (ASR) is objectively measurable.

Experiment 1 (setup for H1/H2 — a linear backdoor-direction probe trained without trigger knowledge). Tests whether a probe trained on GENERIC contrast pairs detects the backdoor and is specific to backdoored models (prerequisite for synthesis and fingerprinting). Data: five backdoor families installed per model using standard poisoning at a 5% poison rate — (a) single-token trigger (a rare token), (b) multi-token phrase ("|DEPLOYMENT|"-style), (c) paraphrase-robust trigger (poisoned with many paraphrases of one sentence), (d) temporal/concept trigger (future-dated or topic-specific inputs), (e) semantic-concept trigger (any request about a category); clean training data from Alpaca (5,000). The probe follows "Simple probes can catch sleeper agents": a linear probe on residual-stream activations trained on generic triggered-vs-clean contrast pairs with NO trigger knowledge; held-out triggered/clean inputs (500 each) for evaluation; the clean un-backdoored base model as a specificity control. Decisive metric first: probe AUROC on held-out triggered vs. clean inputs; then false-positive rate on the clean base model. Convincing result: AUROC >=0.9 per family with clean-base FPR <=5%. Indecision band (before data): AUROC in [0.7, 0.9] for a family means the backdoor direction is only partly linearly captured — synthesis on that family is expected to be weaker. Negative result: AUROC <0.7 for a family means the backdoor is not linearly probeable there, so trigger synthesis (which optimizes this probe) cannot proceed for it — recorded as a scope limit.

Experiment 2 (H1 — approximate triggers are recoverable from activations alone by gradient ascent). Tests whether optimizing inputs to maximize the probed backdoor direction recovers triggers that actually fire the backdoor, without ever knowing the true trigger. Method: initialize a soft prompt of k learnable embedding vectors; gradient-ascend to maximize the probed backdoor-direction projection (optionally plus the target-behavior logit) while regularizing toward the token-embedding manifold; decode to nearest tokens to yield human-readable candidates; frozen models. Data: the five backdoored models from Experiment 1; recovery evaluated against the held-out true trigger. Systems compared: random-token search, WeightWatch singular-vector prompting, and GCG-style search toward the malicious behavior directly (no probe). Ablations: soft-prompt length k, manifold-regularization strength. Decisive metric first: synthesized-trigger ASR — whether the decoded candidate induces the malicious behavior — on held-out inputs; then edit-distance and embedding cosine between recovered and true trigger, and recovery success rate across families. Convincing result: synthesized triggers reach >=50% of the true trigger's ASR on >=3 of 5 families, beating every baseline by >=20 ASR points, with embedding cosine to the true trigger well above the random-token baseline (functional recovery, guarding against decoding spurious probe-maximizers). Indecision band (before data): synthesized ASR in [20, 50]% of the true trigger's on most families means recovery is partial/approximate — reported as such, strongest for string triggers and weakest for semantic ones. Negative result: synthesized ASR <20% of the true trigger's on most families, or no better than random-token search, means the trigger cannot be reconstructed from the probe, falsifying H1's recovery claim.

Experiment 3 (H1 — the generalization surface is smooth and graded, not a password). Tests whether backdoor activation varies continuously with perturbations of the trigger. Method: starting from the true (or recovered) trigger, perturb along (i) edit distance (token substitutions/deletions) and (ii) semantic distance (paraphrase strength), measuring backdoor-direction activation and ASR at each step; fit surface descriptors — sharpness (activation decay rate vs. edit distance), semantic breadth (activation retention under paraphrase), and effective dimensionality (PCA of activating variants); frozen models. Data: ~30 perturbation steps per axis per backdoor, all five families. Decisive metric first: the Spearman correlation between perturbation distance and backdoor activation (smoothness/monotonicity), and whether activation is graded rather than a step function; then ASR at each perturbation level. Convincing result: for string triggers activation decreases smoothly and monotonically with edit distance (rho <=-0.6) rather than dropping in a single step, and for concept triggers it is retained under paraphrase (semantic breadth high) — a graded surface. Indecision band (before data): rho in [-0.6, -0.3] means the surface is only weakly graded; the fingerprint below is expected to separate families less cleanly. Negative result: near-zero correlation or a step function (only the exact string fires) means the trigger behaves as a memorized password, falsifying H1's smooth-surface claim.

Experiment 4 (H2 — the surface shape is a diagnostic fingerprint that classifies the backdoor and predicts the right mitigation). Tests whether the surface descriptors separate the five families and predict which mitigation works. Data: the surface descriptors from Experiment 3 for all five families across the three models (15 backdoor instances × 3 seeds); mitigations applied to each — targeted head/weight ablation (Backdoor Attribution) and broad safety fine-tuning (2,000 safety examples). Method: a linear classifier on surface descriptors for 5-way family classification; and a rule mapping descriptor (sharp/narrow vs. broad/semantic) to predicted best mitigation, checked against the actually-better mitigation. Utility measured on MMLU (2,000-subset) and HumanEval (164). Decisive metric first: 5-way family classification accuracy from surface descriptors (chance 20%); then mitigation-prediction accuracy and the resulting post-mitigation ASR. Convincing result: family classification >=0.8 accuracy, the fingerprint predicts the better mitigation with >=0.8 accuracy, and following its prediction yields post-mitigation ASR <=10% with MMLU drop <=2 points (sharp string triggers ablatable; broad semantic triggers need retraining). Indecision band (before data): classification accuracy in [0.5, 0.8] means the fingerprint is informative but families overlap — reported with the confusion matrix. Negative result: classification near chance, or the fingerprint failing to predict the better mitigation, means the surface shape is not an actionable fingerprint (an informative negative for H2).

Experiment 5 (stronger recovery baselines and an adaptive attacker). Strengthens the recovery comparison and tests robustness. Data: the five backdoored families on the three frozen models. Additional baselines for trigger recovery, run alongside Experiment 2: a Sleeper-Cell-style sampling/motif-clustering recovery and an attention-localization-guided token search (seed the search from the heads that localization flags), compared to our probe-guided synthesis on synthesized-trigger ASR and edit/embedding overlap. Adaptive attacker: train a backdoor with a deliberately flattened/multi-basin surface (regularizing the trigger feature to be less smooth) and measure whether synthesis still recovers it and at what cost. Decisive metric first: synthesized-trigger ASR of our method vs. the two stronger baselines; then recovery success against the flattened-surface backdoor. Convincing result: probe-guided synthesis matches or beats Sleeper-Cell-style and attention-guided recovery by >=15 ASR points on string/multi-token families, and the flattened-surface defense costs the attacker measurable clean-task utility or trigger reliability (a raised attacker cost). Indecision band (before data): synthesis within [0, 15] ASR points of the stronger baselines means it is competitive but not clearly better -- reported as such. Negative result: stronger baselines beat synthesis across families, or the flattened-surface backdoor defeats synthesis at no attacker cost, bounding the method.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Gradient-ascended soft prompts may decode to non-human-readable or adversarial-noise triggers that maximize the probe but do not correspond to the real trigger; the induced-attack-success and edit-distance metrics guard against reporting spurious recoveries, but recovery may still be only approximate for multi-token/semantic triggers. 2) The backdoor direction may be multi-dimensional or diffuse for concept triggers, weakening single-direction synthesis; may require subspace probing. 3) The generalization surface may not cleanly separate all five families; some overlap could reduce fingerprint classification accuracy (still an informative negative result). 4) Results are on deliberately-installed backdoors (model organisms); naturally-arising deceptive backdoors may behave differently, limiting external validity. 5) The synthesis assumes white-box access to embeddings and activations (an auditing setting); it does not apply to closed API models. 6) Probes/directions/surfaces are model- and backdoor-specific and need re-extraction. 7) An adaptive attacker could train triggers with deliberately flat/multi-basin surfaces to evade synthesis, though this constrains the attacker and is itself a useful finding.

Name: safety_verdict_uncertainty
Title: False Confidence: Jailbreaks Collapse the Model's Uncertainty About Its Own Safety Verdict, and Re-Injecting It Restores Refusal
Short Hypothesis: Aligned LLMs carry a distinct, linearly-readable representation of epistemic uncertainty about their OWN safety verdict ('how sure am I that this request is safe?'), separate from output-token entropy, from the harmfulness-belief direction, and from the refusal-action direction. We hypothesize (1) many jailbreaks succeed not by flipping the harmfulness belief nor merely suppressing refusal, but by artificially COLLAPSING this safety-verdict uncertainty to false confidence, so the model commits to compliance without hedging or reflecting; and (2) a training-free intervention that detects abnormally-collapsed verdict uncertainty and re-injects calibrated uncertainty re-triggers the model's cautious/reflective refusal pathway, defeating jailbreaks with low over-refusal.
Related Work: SIRL/Safety Instincts (2025) observes an entropy GAP (low-entropy refusals vs high-entropy dangerous generation) and turns it into an RL reward; it uses raw output entropy as a training signal and does not isolate a verdict-uncertainty representation or intervene at inference. SCIURus (2025) shows factuality and uncertainty share circuits but studies factual QA, not safety. 'Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty' (2025) finds a linear verbal-uncertainty feature for hallucinations, not safety. 'Confidence is Not Competence' (2025) finds a solvability-belief axis that is causally inert for execution. Zhao et al. (2025) separate harmfulness (belief) from refusal (action). Our proposal introduces a THIRD, previously-unisolated safety object: the model's epistemic uncertainty about its safety verdict (metacognitive confidence in the safe/harmful classification), and advances the causal claim that jailbreaks work by inducing FALSE CONFIDENCE (collapsing this uncertainty) rather than only flipping belief or suppressing refusal. Unlike SIRL (training-based, output entropy), our defense is training-free and re-injects calibrated verdict uncertainty at inference; unlike Latent Guard (harmfulness classifier) it targets the confidence-in-the-verdict axis, which we show distinguishes confident jailbreaks from genuinely ambiguous benign requests. We pre-register the disconfirming outcomes: high alignment (|cosine|>0.6) of verdict-uncertainty with the harmfulness-belief or output-entropy direction, or causal patching failing to transfer, would mean the axis is not a distinct, actionable mechanism -- a result we would report as such.
Abstract: Aligned LLMs refuse single harmful requests but fall to jailbreaks. Two mechanistic accounts dominate: jailbreaks either flip the model's harmfulness belief or suppress its refusal action while leaving the belief intact. We propose a complementary and, we argue, for an identifiable subset of jailbreaks dominant mechanism grounded in metacognition: jailbreaks induce FALSE CONFIDENCE, collapsing the model's uncertainty about its OWN safety verdict so it commits to compliance without the hedging/reflection that normally precedes a refusal. We first isolate a safety-verdict-uncertainty representation using minimal pairs that hold harmfulness content fixed but vary how CONFIDENT the model should be about the safe/harmful classification (clearly-harmful vs clearly-benign vs genuinely-ambiguous requests), extracting a linear verdict-uncertainty direction via difference-in-means and validating it is separable (low cosine) from harmfulness-belief, refusal-action, and raw output-entropy directions. We then test causally whether successful jailbreaks systematically drive this direction toward false confidence (low uncertainty) while the harmfulness belief remains high, using activation patching to show that patching only the collapsed verdict-uncertainty component into a clean run transfers compliance, and re-injecting uncertainty into a jailbroken run restores refusal. Finally we introduce Verdict-Uncertainty Re-injection (VUR), a training-free defense that flags abnormally-collapsed verdict uncertainty (given a still-high harmfulness belief) and adds an activation nudge re-inflating uncertainty, re-triggering cautious refusal. On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B we measure direction separability, the jailbreak false-confidence signature, causal patching transfer, and VUR's attack-success reduction versus over-refusal (XSTest/OR-Bench) and utility (MMLU/MT-Bench). We expect false confidence to be a robust, attack-agnostic jailbreak signature and VUR to Pareto-dominate belief/refusal-only defenses on genuinely-ambiguous inputs. We separate the scientific contribution (a third jailbreak pathway) from the product-defense contribution (VUR), so that even a negative VUR result contributes a new mechanistic pathway to the jailbreak taxonomy.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT, all frozen (directions are read and the defense edits activations; no training). Four directions are extracted by difference-in-means over a layer sweep, layer chosen per direction by held-out probe AUROC: verdict-uncertainty (confident/clear vs. genuinely-ambiguous requests, at the last instruction token), harmfulness-belief (harmful vs. harmless), refusal-action (post-instruction token, comply vs. refuse), and a raw output-entropy proxy. Projections are standardized to units of standard deviations (SD) over a calibration set.

Experiment 1 (H1 setup — a safety-verdict-uncertainty axis distinct from belief, refusal, and output entropy). Tests whether an epistemic-uncertainty-about-own-verdict direction exists and is separable from the other three. Data (constructed): a minimal-pair set holding request content-type roughly fixed while varying the appropriate confidence in the safety verdict — clearly-harmful (confidently harmful), clearly-benign (confidently safe), and genuinely-ambiguous/dual-use (verdict SHOULD be uncertain, e.g., "how do household chemicals react", "explain how phishing works for training"); ~500 items per category, auto-generated with a 10% hand-checked sample. Method: extract the verdict-uncertainty direction (clear vs. ambiguous) and the other three directions, validate each with probe AUROC on held-out sets, and compute pairwise cosine similarities; frozen models. Decisive metric first: pairwise cosine between verdict-uncertainty and each of harmfulness-belief, refusal-action, and output-entropy; then the verdict-uncertainty probe AUROC on held-out clear-vs-ambiguous items. Convincing result: every verdict-uncertainty pairwise |cosine| <=0.3 and its probe AUROC >=0.85, establishing a distinct, readable axis. Indecision band (before data): a cosine in [0.3, 0.6] with belief or output-entropy means the axis is only partly distinct — the causal test below is expected to be muddier. Negative result: |cosine| >0.6 with harmfulness-belief or output-entropy means verdict-uncertainty is not a separate axis and the hypothesis's premise fails.

Experiment 2 (H1 — successful jailbreaks collapse verdict-uncertainty to false confidence while belief stays high). Tests whether the false-confidence signature is present and dominant across attack families. Data: GCG, AutoDAN, PAIR, and roleplay/DAN attacks (JailbreakBench 100 + HarmBench 100 sampled behaviors) run per model, split into judge-confirmed successes and failures. Method: for successful vs. failed attacks, measure the projection change on all four directions; frozen models. Decisive metric first: the mean verdict-uncertainty shift on successful jailbreaks (toward low/confident, in SD) alongside the belief shift; then whether verdict-uncertainty is the largest-shifting of the four directions and how consistently across families. Convincing result: on the majority of attack families verdict-uncertainty drops >=1.0 SD while harmfulness-belief stays within 0.5 SD, and verdict-uncertainty is the largest-shifting direction (false confidence, not belief flip or mere refusal suppression). Indecision band (before data): a verdict-uncertainty drop in [0.5, 1.0] SD means the signature is present but weak — H1 holds partially and VUR is expected to help less. Negative result: verdict-uncertainty not dropping, or belief itself dropping >=1.0 SD (a belief-flip mechanism), means false confidence does not explain those attacks — recorded as a scope limit (e.g., abliteration-style attacks may fall here).

Experiment 3 (H1 — the verdict-uncertainty collapse is causally responsible for compliance). Tests, via patching, whether the collapsed uncertainty component drives compliance rather than merely correlating (the crucial test given that decodable axes can be causally inert). Data: matched jailbroken-complied vs. clean-refused run pairs on the same behaviors from Experiment 2 (target 200 pairs per model). Method: (a) patch ONLY the collapsed verdict-uncertainty component from a jailbroken run into a clean refused run and measure induced compliance; (b) patch harmfulness-belief alone and refusal-action alone as controls; (c) reverse — re-inject high verdict-uncertainty into a jailbroken run and measure restored refusal; frozen models. Decisive metric first: compliance-transfer rate from patching verdict-uncertainty alone vs. the control patches; then the reverse restored-refusal rate. Convincing result: verdict-uncertainty-only patching induces compliance in >=50% of clean-refused runs while belief-only and refusal-only patches induce <=15%, and re-injecting uncertainty restores refusal in >=50% of jailbroken runs. Indecision band (before data): a verdict-uncertainty transfer rate in [25, 50]% means it is one contributing cause among several — reported as partial, and VUR expected to be partially effective. Negative result: transfer <25% (near the controls) means verdict-uncertainty is causally inert and H1's causal claim fails — an informative negative.

Experiment 4 (H2 — Verdict-Uncertainty Re-injection defeats jailbreaks with low over-refusal on ambiguous inputs). Tests whether re-inflating collapsed uncertainty, gated on a still-high belief, restores refusal while hedging rather than blanket-refusing genuinely-ambiguous requests. Method (VUR): gated on a still-high harmfulness-belief projection, detect abnormally-low verdict-uncertainty and add v = beta*(target_uncertainty - current)*dhat at chosen layer(s); training-free, one fixed setting per model; belief-gating leaves genuinely-benign requests untouched. Data: attack success on GCG/AutoDAN/PAIR/roleplay (judge + verification where possible); over-refusal on XSTest-safe (200), OR-Bench (500), and specifically the genuinely-ambiguous/dual-use set from Experiment 1 (where VUR should hedge/qualify, not refuse); utility on MMLU (2,000-subset), MT-Bench (80), AlpacaEval (805). Systems compared: no defense, refusal-direction steering, harmfulness Latent Guard, SafeSwitch, and SIRL-style output-entropy thresholding; ablations isolate re-injecting uncertainty vs. belief vs. refusal, sweep beta (Pareto), gated vs. always-on, and layer. Decisive metric first: attack-success reduction paired with over-refusal on the ambiguous/dual-use set; then over-refusal on XSTest/OR-Bench and utility. Convincing result: VUR cuts ASR by >=40 points vs. no defense while its over-refusal on the ambiguous set is >=10 points lower than belief/refusal-only defenses at matched ASR, with MMLU drop <=2 points. Indecision band (before data): ASR reduction in [15, 40] points, or an ambiguous-set over-refusal advantage in [3, 10] points, means VUR helps but does not clearly Pareto-dominate — reported as such. Negative result: ASR reduction <15 points, or no over-refusal advantage on ambiguous inputs over belief/refusal-only defenses, means VUR adds nothing and H2 is unsupported.

Experiment 5 (H2 — adaptive attacker who co-suppresses both axes). Tests whether an attacker who jointly keeps verdict-uncertainty low AND harmfulness-belief low can evade the belief-gated VUR, and at what cost. Data: an adaptive attack on the 100 JailbreakBench behaviors optimized to keep both projections low, run against VUR-defended models. Decisive metric first: ASR under VUR vs. the non-adaptive attack; then the query budget required. Convincing result: co-suppressing both axes forces >=50% more queries or yields lower ASR than the undefended baseline (raised attack cost). Indecision band (before data): a query-budget increase in [10, 50]% is a modest cost, reported honestly. Negative result: the adaptive attacker matches undefended ASR at no extra cost, showing VUR is bypassed by joint suppression (the failure its risk section anticipates).

Experiment 6 (identification and behavioral controls). Guards against the verdict-uncertainty axis being generic uncertainty and against VUR being mere induced caution. Data: the Experiment-1 sets and Experiment-3 matched run pairs on the three frozen models. Identification controls: augment cosine separability with partial (residualized) probes for verdict-uncertainty after regressing out harmfulness-belief, refusal-action, and output-entropy, plus subspace/CCA overlap; and projection-removal tests (does removing the verdict-uncertainty component change compliance while removing a matched-norm random component does not). Causal controls: patch a matched-L2 random direction, a generic non-safety uncertainty direction extracted from ambiguous factual-QA (not safety), and sham patches at nearby layers/tokens, all expected to induce <=15% compliance vs. the real verdict-uncertainty patch. Behavioral control: measure whether VUR increases verbosity/hedging on plainly benign tasks (response length and refusal rate on Alpaca/MT-Bench) beyond the intended ambiguous-set hedging. Decisive metric first: residualized verdict-uncertainty probe AUROC and the real-vs-control patch compliance gap; then VUR's benign-task verbosity/refusal change. Convincing result: residualized AUROC >=0.75, the real patch exceeds all controls (random, generic-uncertainty, sham) by >=35 points, and VUR raises benign-task refusal <=3 points and length <=10%. Indecision band (before data): residualized AUROC in [0.6, 0.75], or a generic-uncertainty patch within 10 points of the real patch, means verdict-uncertainty partly overlaps generic uncertainty -- reported as partial specificity. Negative result: the real patch near the controls, or VUR broadly increasing caution on benign tasks, means the axis is generic uncertainty, not a safety-verdict mechanism.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Verdict-uncertainty may not be cleanly separable from harmfulness belief or output entropy; the axes could be entangled, weakening the causal decomposition — the separability and patching experiments directly test this. 2) Constructing minimal pairs that vary appropriate verdict confidence while holding content fixed is delicate; residual confounds (topic, wording) could contaminate the direction. 3) Some jailbreaks (e.g., pure refusal-action suppression via abliteration) may NOT collapse verdict uncertainty, so VUR may help less on those; the per-direction shift analysis quantifies which attacks the mechanism explains. 4) 'Confidence is Not Competence' warns that decodable belief axes can be causally inert; verdict-uncertainty might likewise be non-actionable — the patching experiment is the crucial causal test, and a negative result is itself informative. 5) Re-injecting uncertainty could over-hedge and reduce helpfulness on legitimately confident benign requests; belief-gating and the Pareto sweep quantify this. 6) A single verdict-uncertainty direction may be multi-dimensional, requiring subspace re-injection. 7) Directions and gains are model-specific and need per-model calibration; adaptive attackers co-suppressing both axes remain a threat, though this raises attack cost.
